idiom_name: const cache = new Map() inside a memoize() factory
implementation_notes: A closure around a Map is the JavaScript form of the pattern: the memo is private to the returned function, Map accepts any value as a key with no prototype keys to collide with, and MDN notes that Map is the safe choice when keys or values come from user input. Use has() before get() so a stored undefined is still a hit, and derive the key explicitly for multi-argument functions - JavaScript has no structural key, so a tuple, a canonical string or nested Maps are the options. The classic decorator class is only worth writing when the cache needs a public surface (clear, size, stats) or must be shared by several functions; for a single function the closure replaces it completely.
pitfalls: Map compares object keys by identity (MDN), so two structurally equal argument objects are two entries; canonicalise to a primitive key or accept the misses.
A memo created inside the function body (per call) has no lifetime and silently disables caching - hoist it to module or component scope.
The cache holds strong references to keys and results, so long-lived caches keyed by request data grow the process; bound them or key them weakly.
Returning the cached object hands every caller the same mutable instance: callers that mutate the result corrupt the cache for everyone else.

variants.name: WeakMap keyed by object identity (entries die with their keys)
variants.idiom_name: const memo = new WeakMap() for per-object derived data
variants.implementation_notes: When the key is an object - a DOM node, a component instance, a parse node - and the derived value should not outlive it, WeakMap is the store: it does not create strong references to its keys, so a collected key makes its entry collectable too (MDN also notes that newly added engines document a getOrInsertComputed helper for the compute-on-miss case). That removes the most common JavaScript memo leak at the price of introspection: WeakMap keys are not enumerable, so there is no size, no iteration and no clear. Use it for metadata and derived per-object views; use Map when the cache itself must be observable, invalidatable or bounded.
pitfalls: WeakMap is not enumerable and has no size or clear, so it cannot implement an LRU or report hit rates - the tradeoff for not retaining keys.
Primitive keys are rejected (only objects and non-registered symbols are allowed), so a memoized function of strings needs a Map instead.
An entry is gone as soon as its key is unreachable, so a caller that only keeps the value (not the key) loses the cache silently and recomputes.
Sharing one WeakMap across modules is still shared mutable state: concurrent interleaved async code can compute twice, since neither Map nor WeakMap offers atomic compute-if-absent.

variants.name: Bounded LRU memo built on Map insertion order
variants.idiom_name: Map with delete+set recency refresh and first-key eviction
variants.implementation_notes: Map preserves insertion order, which is enough to build a least-recently-used bound without a library: on a hit, delete and re-set the key to move it to the newest end, and when the size exceeds the cap, evict the oldest key via keys().next().value. That makes the memo safe for unbounded key domains, which is the honest requirement for anything keyed by request data, and it keeps the policy visible in the code instead of hidden in a dependency. Reach for a library (lru-cache, memoizee) once the policy grows weights, TTL, stale-while-revalidate or metrics; the hand-rolled form is the smallest correct answer before that.
pitfalls: Eviction means recomputation, not staleness: a wrongly sized cap turns a fast path into a slower one than no cache at all, so the hit rate has to be measured.
delete+set on every hit mutates the cache during iteration if the surrounding code is iterating it - keep the cache private to the wrapper.
The cap counts keys, not memory: large results under few keys still blow the budget, so weight-based policies need the library forms.
Async callers racing on the same key can both miss and both compute; a Map has no atomic compute-if-absent, so deduplicate in flight separately if that matters.
